chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Adam ibn Ishaq, from a man from our companions, from Abdul Hameed ibn Ismail, who said:

I asked Abu Abdullah (peace be upon him) about a man who had a slave girl whom he slept with, and she used to go out regarding his needs. So she became pregnant, and he feared that the child may not be from him. How should he deal with it? Should he sell the slave girl and the child? He (peace be upon him) said: He sells the slave girl but does not sell the child, and he does not inherit him anything from his inheritance.

key_terms.أَلَا يَكُونَ مِنْهُ: That it may not be from him (paternity doubt)
key_terms.يَطَؤُهَا: He sleeps with her / has sexual relations with her

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on selling a pregnant slave girl and her child if the master doubts paternity?
ai.summary: This ruling from Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies the status of the *Umm al-Walad* (mother of the child) in Shia jurisprudence, establishing that the child is free and legitimate but does not inherit from the father's estate unless specified, distinguishing it from the Sunni view of direct inheritance. The master's sale of the slave girl severs her bond with him, while the child remains independent, highlighting the principle that paternity is established by the master's act of intercourse (*Istirqaq*) even if he later doubts it. This hadith is foundational for understanding the legal mechanics of manumission and inheritance rights for concubine-born children in Shia fiqh.
